items.title: Learned surrogates for particle-resolved suspension flows
items.subtitle: Current Ph.D. research in the SmartDATA Lab with Dr. Joel B. Harley: predicting the flow around hundreds to a thousand settling particles from a learned one-particle disturbance, summed over neighbours, instead of rerunning the particle-resolved simulation.

items.desc: Ph.D. research in the SmartDATA Lab: a superposition surrogate for particle-resolved simulations of settling suspensions, evaluated with pre-registered, held-out tests.

details.overview: Particle-resolved simulations of settling suspensions resolve the flow around every particle, at hours of compute per case. This project learns the velocity disturbance a single particle induces, with one network shared by all particles and built to respect rotations and reflections, and predicts the fluid velocity anywhere as the sum of those disturbances over the nearest particles. Evaluation is treated as a research object in its own right: locked test snapshots, pre-registered comparisons, held-out flow regimes, and analyses of what the network has learned.
details.status: Active research since Fall 2025 · results written up in the research log (October 2026 onward).
collaborators: SmartDATA Lab, University of Florida — Dr. Joel B. Harley (advisor)

writeup.lead: A particle-resolved simulation of 1,000 settling particles takes hours per case. This project asks how much of that flow a learned model can predict from the particles alone — and builds the evaluation needed to know when to trust it.

sections.heading: The problem: flow around many particles
body: Particle-resolved direct numerical simulation (PR-DNS) of a settling suspension resolves the fluid between every particle. It is the reference for drag and mixing models in particle-laden flows, and it is expensive: each case is a large solver run, and the dataset this project uses spans 46 cases across density ratio, volume fraction and Reynolds number, with up to 1,000 particles each.
The surrogate's job is to reproduce the fluid velocity (and, in current work, the pressure) at any point, given only the particles' positions and states, without running the solver.

sections.heading: The model: one particle's disturbance, summed
body: One shared network maps a particle's state and the offset to a fluid point to the velocity that particle induces there. The predicted flow is the sum of those disturbances over the nearest particles. The network is equivariant: rotating or reflecting the whole configuration rotates or reflects the prediction, by construction.

Two architectures are compared: the original per-particle network, which needs an iterative self-consistent update of the particle states to capture many-body effects, and an invariant-attention transformer that lets each particle's disturbance depend on its neighbours directly.

figure.caption: Figure 1 — Each particle contributes a learned disturbance computed by one shared equivariant network; the flow is their sum over nearby particles, and the result is audited on held-out regimes and against full-resolution surface forces.

sections.heading: How it is evaluated
body: The test snapshots stay locked until a pre-registered evaluation; development comparisons are written down before they are run. The questions are about generalization and trust, not just pointwise error:
bullets: **Held-out regimes** — train on all cases except one density ratio, volume fraction or Reynolds number, or except one case, and predict the held-out ones.
**Architecture comparisons** — the original network against attention-based variants, across seeds, under the same budget.
**What the model learned** — probes of the attention, neighbour-removal tests, and the learned one-particle disturbance compared with the textbook flow around an isolated sphere.
**Stability** — when the self-consistent state update converges, when it drifts, and how to stop it.

sections.heading: Current work: pressure and physical consistency
body: The same superposition idea extends to the pressure field, and the velocity can be made to conserve mass by construction. Together they give each particle's hydrodynamic force from the model, which is being checked against full-resolution simulation fields — a step toward a surrogate that can move the particles, not only describe the flow around them.

sections.heading: Where it stands
body: Results so far are written up in the research log: [Superposing learned one-particle flows](../notes/superposing-learned-one-particle-flows.html), [Inputs before capacity](../notes/inputs-before-capacity.html), [When converging is the wrong goal](../notes/when-converging-is-the-wrong-goal.html) and [A research loop across two clusters](../notes/a-research-loop-across-two-clusters.html).

faq.q: What is a surrogate model here?
faq.a: A machine-learning model trained on the output of an expensive particle-resolved simulation, so it can predict the flow for a new particle configuration without rerunning the solver. The simulation stays the ground truth; the surrogate is checked against it on snapshots and flow regimes it never trained on.

faq.q: Why build the flow from one-particle disturbances?
faq.a: A particle's effect on the fluid around it is the physically natural unit, and it is the same for every particle up to its state and surroundings. Learning it once and summing over neighbours keeps the model small, makes it work for any number of particles, and makes what it learned inspectable: the learned disturbance can be compared directly with the textbook flow around a single sphere.

faq.q: Is any of this work public yet?
faq.a: Yes: results are written up in the research log, linked under "Where it stands" above. Code and papers will be linked here when they are released.

glossary.definition: Numerical simulation of fluid flow by solving the governing equations (such as Navier–Stokes) over a discretized domain.
A fast learned approximation of an expensive simulation, trained on the simulation's inputs and outputs.
Feeding a model's own predictions back as inputs for the next step; the standard stress test for learned dynamics.
A simulation that resolves the fluid flow around every individual particle, rather than modelling the particles' effect on average.
A model property: transforming the input (here, rotating or reflecting the particle configuration) transforms the output in the same way.
